text: I'M JOEL BENOIT. I'M THE CIVIL DIVISION CHIEF AT THE STATE'S ATTORNEY'S OFFICE. THE TWO ISSUES I WILL BRIEFLY ADDRESS ARE, ONE, financial assurance for decommissioning as a condition of zoning approval for data storage centers, and secondly, whether enacting a moratorium on data storage centers has any legal effect. Each board member has been provided with a memo from Attorney Anthony Licata of TAF Law. TAF Law, with 1,100 attorneys working throughout the country, is nationally recognized. for its expertise in land use and zoning matters. And Mr. Licata of its Chicago office has over 35 years' experience with these matters. The State's Attorney's Office asked Mr. Licata to provide insight as to whether nationally financial assurance is required for such projects and also issues the Board should consider when deciding whether to enact a financial assurance requirement for these type of projects. Now, each board member has been given that report and should carefully consider the TAP memo as a whole. But the main takeaway from the memo is that no other governmental bodies require financial assurance for these types of projects. And were Sangamon County to require such financial assurance, it would incentivize developers to construct their projects in other jurisdictions, thereby depriving Sangamon County of the benefits OF THIS PROPOSED PROJECT. AS TO THE MORATORIUM ISSUE, I'M KIND OF REPEATING MYSELF, AND SOME OF YOU MAY HAVE HEARD THIS BEFORE AT THE COUNTY BOARD MEETING, BUT I'VE BEEN ASKED TO SHARE MY OPINION ON THE LEGAL EFFECT OF THE COUNTY ENACTING A MORATORIUM PROVIDING THAT NO REQUEST FOR DATA STORAGE CENTER ZONING APPROVALS WOULD BE CONSIDERED UNTIL THE COUNTY ENACTS NEW RULES GOVERNING THE ZONING OF SUCH PROJECTS. such a moratorium would have no legal effect. Everyone would be entitled to continue to rely on the existing zoning rules. Now it's true that no one has the right to the continuation of existing zoning laws. However, rights under existing zoning laws vest when a person reasonably believes they will be allowed to develop property under existing law and this REASONABLE BELIEF RISES BECAUSE NO OFFICIAL ACTION HAS TAKEN PLACE TO CHANGE THE EXISTING LAW. AND SECONDLY, THEY HAVE SUBSTANTIALLY CHANGED THEIR POSITION. AN EXAMPLE OF THAT IS INCURRING SUBSTANTIAL EXPENSES BASED ON THIS REASONABLE BELIEF. SO THE ONLY WAY THE COUNTY CAN PREVENT PEOPLE FROM ALIGNING ON EXISTING ZONING RULES IS TO FORMALLY START THE PROCESS OF CHANGING THE EXISTING LAW. Amending the county zoning ordinance requires a text amendment pursuant to Illinois statute. This involves introducing proposed amendments before the zoning committee, which if approved, they next go before the zoning board of appeals, and then finally they're considered by the county board. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My name is Kyle Berry. I'm an attorney with McGuire Woods, and I'm representing the petitioner here tonight. I live here in Springfield. I'm a Sangamon County resident and taxpayer, and my office is about four blocks away here. I just want to discuss a couple legal issues that were just raised. First of all, neither Mr. Davis nor Mr. Applegate attended the public hearing last month in front of the Zoning Board of Appeals. I don't know why. You'll have to ask them. But that was an evidentiary hearing. And the reason that the state law and your ordinance requires a public hearing that's an evidentiary hearing is that witnesses testify they're under oath. They make statements. And when people do that, they tend to be a little more careful about what they say, or they should. And evidence is considered. Well, the zoning board considered the evidence and they voted five to zero to recommend approval. The evidence that was submitted here tonight, anything that's new, shouldn't be considered under the law because it was supposed to be done at the evidentiary hearing. Makes sense, right? So when it comes to data centers generally and the arguments that data centers are bad, the problem with that argument is that this board, this county, adopted a data center siting standard last July. And 25 years ago, the Illinois Supreme Court said that once a permitting body adopts a standard and sets something up as a special or conditional use, then it essentially has made a determination that that use is compatible with the zoning district that is being proposed in. In this case, at the agricultural zoning district. And so the approval, if the applicant meets the standards, then the permitting authority is under the law, under the Supreme Court ruling, not my opinion, it's the Supreme Court's, the body is required to approve the ordinance, approve the petition if it meets the standards. Well, in this case, as Mr. Howe already indicated, the petitioner has met those standards in the application and in the evidentiary hearing. By the way, the commitments that were made at the evidentiary hearing are binding. That was a recorded meeting. The planning staff has found that the petitioners met those standards. And then the zoning board, again, voted to recommend five to zero unanimously that those standards had been met. So, again, I just wanted to make it clear that while the arguments that were made that you're not required to consider that, I beg to differ. The hearing was made. The hearing was properly noticed under Illinois law. And the zoning board has made its recommendation. It's in front of you. And, you know, they can ask you to delay it. This is a common – I do a lot of hearings around the state. I've appeared in about half the counties, mostly on renewable energy projects. It's a common tactic of opponents to ask for a delay because they know that delays can kill a project. So, again, I'll turn things over to Mr. Hout again, but I wanted to address those legal issues. Thank you.
